title: The First Believers
subtitle: The Vanguard of Faith and the Dawn of the Community
summary: The quiet dawn of Islam in Makkah, the immediate acceptance by Khadijah, the youth Ali ibn Abi Talib, the freedman Zayd ibn Harithah, the esteemed Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and the core group of noble companions who embraced the truth through Abu Bakr's early outreach.

sections.text: The Dawn of Faith in the Household of Prophethood

Following the divine summons to arise and warn, the proclamation of Islam commenced quietly and discreetly within the immediate circle of those who knew Muhammad's character most intimately. In the privacy of his home, faith was born not through political rhetoric or social agitation, but through the profound, unhesitating conviction of those who had witnessed his flawless truthfulness for decades.

First of all people to embrace Islam, according to the great majority of scholars, was Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. She believed in the message as soon as it was related to her, comforted the Prophet, affirmed his mission, and stood beside him as he offered the earliest prayers.
Ali ibn Abi Talib and Zayd ibn Harithah

Within the same household lived 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's young cousin; Ibn Ishaq gives his age as about ten, and other ages are reported. Having entered Muhammad's care during a year of hardship, 'Ali had grown up under his guidance. Ibn Ishaq relates that 'Ali came upon Muhammad and Khadijah while they were praying.

In Ibn Ishaq's account, when 'Ali asked about their worship, Muhammad explained the call to worship God alone without partners and invited him to believe. 'Ali waited until the next morning and then declared his faith, becoming the first child to accept Islam. Later scholars often noted that he had never worshipped an idol.

Zayd ibn Harithah, the Prophet's freedman and adopted son, also embraced the faith among the very first. He had earlier chosen to remain with Muhammad rather than return to his own family, and he is counted as the first freedman to accept Islam.
The quiet night sky over the desert sanctuary of Makkah where the first prayers of Islam were offered.
Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: The Peerless Companion

Beyond the Prophet's household, the first adult free man to embrace Islam, on the view of most scholars, was his close friend 'Abdullah ibn Abi Quhafah, known as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. A respected merchant of the clan of Banu Taym, Abu Bakr was known in Makkah for his knowledge of genealogy, his gentle manners and his generosity.

Abu Bakr accepted Islam as soon as the Prophet presented it to him. Ibn Ishaq relates a saying of the Prophet about this, through a chain that does not reach back to the events in connected form; hadith scholars therefore regard it as weak, although the meaning is widely cited.

"I never invited anyone to Islam without his showing some reluctance, hesitation and deliberation, except Abu Bakr; he did not hold back when I mentioned it to him, nor did he hesitate." — Ibn Ishaq, through Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Tamimi (a disconnected chain); in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham and al-Bayhaqi's Dala'il al-Nubuwwah

An authentic report gives a sense of how small the community was in its first days. 'Ammar ibn Yasir, himself an early Muslim, described what he saw. Commentators identify the two women as Khadijah and either Umm Ayman or Sumayyah, and differ over the names of the five slaves; they also explain that 'Ammar was speaking of those whose Islam he knew of, since others kept their faith hidden.
"I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ when there was no one with him but five slaves, two women, and Abu Bakr." — 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 3660
The Vanguard Brought by Abu Bakr

Abu Bakr did not keep his faith to himself. Ibn Ishaq relates that he began inviting men of his people whom he trusted, and that through him, in this early period, five men accepted Islam who would later be counted among the Ten Promised Paradise (al-'Asharah al-Mubashsharun):

'Uthman ibn 'Affan of Banu Umayyah, a wealthy and very modest merchant; al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam of Banu Asad, the son of the Prophet's aunt Safiyyah; 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf of Banu Zuhrah; Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas of Banu Zuhrah, the clan of the Prophet's mother; and Talhah ibn 'Ubaydillah of Banu Taym. Abu Bakr brought them to the Prophet, and they accepted Islam.
The rocky paths and quiet quarters of Makkah where the earliest believers gathered in secret.
The Emerging Brotherhood Across Social Divides

Others soon followed: Abu 'Ubaydah 'Amir ibn al-Jarrah, whom the Prophet later called the 'Trustworthy One of this Nation' in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari; al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam, whose house would become the meeting place of the believers; 'Uthman ibn Maz'un; Sa'id ibn Zayd and his wife Fatimah bint al-Khattab; and Asma' bint Abi Bakr.

The message also reached the poor, the enslaved and the foreigners of Makkah: Bilal ibn Rabah, the Abyssinian; Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, the blacksmith; and Suhayb ibn Sinan, known as al-Rumi. Within this small community, faith, not lineage, became the measure of a person.

These early Muslims kept their faith hidden. Ibn Ishaq relates that when they wanted to pray they would go out to the ravines around Makkah, out of sight of their people. Some early reports state that before the five daily prayers were prescribed, they prayed two units in the morning and two in the evening, though scholars differ over the form of prayer at this stage.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas later recalled how few they were in those days: 'No one accepted Islam except on the day I accepted it, and I remained for seven days as a third of Islam' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Hadith 3727). Ibn Hajar explains that Sa'd was speaking of what he knew at the time, since others kept their Islam hidden.
